A_target.statement:
Let $f$ be [[Definition:Continuous Real Function|continuous]] on $\closedint a b$.
Then $f$ is [[Definition:Bounded Real-Valued Function|bounded]] and there exists $x^* \in \closedint a b$ with:
:$\map f {x^*} = \displaystyle \sup_{x \mathop \in \closedint a b} \map f x$

B_source.statement: Every [[Definition:Bounded Real Sequence|bounded real sequence]] has a [[Definition:Convergent Real Sequence|convergent]] [[Definition:Subsequence|subsequence]].

substitutions.an arbitrary bounded sequence: a sequence of points where f is large
substitutions.the convergent subsequence: a subsequence converging to a candidate maximizer

derived.the limit point: the point where the supremum is attained

object_map.reformulation: Reduce attainment of the supremum to extracting a convergent subsequence from a maximizing sequence.

validity_conditions: The interval must be closed so that the limit of the subsequence stays in the domain.
Continuity transfers the values along the subsequence to the limit point.
proof_plan:
{{AimForCont}} $f$ is unbounded above, and choose $x_n \in \closedint a b$ with $\map f {x_n} > n$.
By the [[Bolzano-Weierstrass Theorem]], a subsequence $x_{n_k}$ converges to some $x$, which lies in $\closedint a b$ as the interval is [[Definition:Closed Real Interval|closed]].

By continuity $\map f {x_{n_k} } \to \map f x$, contradicting $\map f {x_{n_k} } > n_k \to \infty$.
Hence $f$ is bounded above, and $M = \sup f$ exists.

Choose $x_n$ with $\map f {x_n} > M - \dfrac 1 n$.
By the [[Bolzano-Weierstrass Theorem]] again, a subsequence converges to some $x^* \in \closedint a b$.

By continuity, $\map f {x^*} = \lim \map f {x_{n_k} } \ge M$, so $\map f {x^*} = M$.
Applying this to $-f$ gives boundedness below and attainment of the infimum.
This is the [[Extreme Value Theorem]].
{{qed}}
